UPOAA.note: Florida Power of Attorney Act, ch. 709 Part II (ch. 2011-210), a state act with UPOAA-like structure but material departures; formal UPOAA enactment status not verified on uniformlaws.org

UHCDA.note: Florida uses ch. 765 (health care advance directives; surrogate and proxy)

UGCOPAA.note: Florida guardianship is ch. 744; guardian advocates ch. 393

UPC.note: Florida Probate Code (chs. 731-735) is state-specific; UPC enactment status not verified

UTC.note: Florida Trust Code, ch. 736, uses UTC section numbering; enactment status not verified on uniformlaws.org

RUFADAA.note: Florida Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act, ch. 740 (ch. 2016-46), tracks RUFADAA text with Florida modifications

RUAGA.note: Anatomical gifts are in ch. 765 Part V; priority list differs from Revised UAGA §9

patches.diff: Differs from UPOAA: (1) a power is durable only if it contains durability language (UPOAA §104 makes durability the default); (2) execution requires two witnesses plus notary; (3) new springing powers are void (see financial-poa-springing); (4) filing an incapacity/guardian-advocate petition suspends the power, and adjudication of incapacity terminates it unless the court preserves authority (UPOAA does not terminate on guardianship); (5) general 'all acts' grants confer no authority, each power must be specifically granted; (6) financial institutions presumptively have 4 business days to accept or reject for banking/investment transactions, and may demand an agent affidavit.

patches.diff: Florida uses a 'health care surrogate' designation (ch. 765 Part II) rather than the UHCDA power of attorney for health care. Execution requires two adult witnesses with relationship limits. By default authority begins only on a physician's incapacity determination and lapses if capacity returns, but the principal may make it immediately exercisable. Revocation may be oral and takes effect when communicated. An agent under a durable POA may also hold health care powers if specifically granted, and an incapacity proceeding does not suspend those powers. The surrogate survives guardianship unless the court modifies it (§744.3115).

patches.diff: Florida's proxy list (§765.401) differs from UHCDA §5. It puts a previously appointed guardian first, lists parents ahead of siblings, uses majority rule for adult children and siblings, adds an adult relative who has shown special care and concern, a close friend, and a bioethics-committee-selected clinical social worker as last resort, and requires clear and convincing evidence to withhold or withdraw life-prolonging procedures. UHCDA lets a patient orally designate a surrogate. That route was not found in §765.401.

patches.diff: Florida has no UPC §3-1201 style small-estate affidavit usable with anyone who holds the property. The only affidavit route is §735.303: payment of up to $2,000 in sole-name accounts at one institution to a family member, no sooner than 6 months after death (limit raised from $1,000 by ch. 2026-57). Larger small estates go through court: summary administration (§735.201, now up to $150,000; raised from $75,000 effective July 1, 2026) or disposition without administration (§735.301). An order of summary administration also works as fiduciary credentials under ch. 740.

transitions.event: Class member gives all or part of body
conditions: No actual notice of contrary indications by decedent
No actual notice of opposition by a member of a prior class

patches.diff: Section 765.512 differs from Revised UAGA §9. A designated health care surrogate may make the gift. The fallback list runs spouse, adult children, parents, adult siblings, adult grandchildren, grandparents, close personal friend, guardian of the person, then a court-appointed representative ad litem, and Revised UAGA's 'adult who exhibited special care and concern' class is absent. Florida's formal adoption of Revised UAGA was not verified.

patches.name: Legally authorized person to direct disposition of remains
patches.summary: The person with legal authority to authorize and direct disposition of a decedent's remains, including cremation, under Florida's funeral and cemetery law.

assigned.event: Priority: (1) decedent's own written inter vivos authorization; (2) DD Form 93 designee if decedent died in military service; (3) surviving spouse; (4) adult child; (5) parent; (6) adult sibling; (7) adult grandchild; (8) grandparent; (9) next degree of kinship; if none, fallback includes guardian at death, PR, attorney in fact at death, health surrogate at death, public officials, institution, or a willing friend

ends.event: Cremated remains unclaimed 90 days after cremation: establishment may dispose
Final disposition completed (statute does not state an explicit end point)

states.label: No written directions; priority determined at death
Decedent left written inter vivos authorization or DD Form 93 designation

transitions.event: Decedent provides written inter vivos authorizations and directions
conditions: Before letters, any person may carry out decedent's written body/funeral instructions

transitions.event: Death: highest available priority class becomes legally authorized person
conditions: Funeral establishment may rely on any one member of a class who represents no known objection by same or higher class (cremation)

transitions.event: Person arrested for domestic violence against the deceased or an act that caused or contributed to death is accorded no interest
Legally authorized person gives written cremation authorization and declaration of intent for cremated remains
conditions: Division of cremated remains requires LAP consent; disputes go to court

transitions.event: No family exists or is available for unclaimed remains: licensed funeral director may assume LAP responsibility; county may authorize burial or cremation
Final disposition carried out

patches.diff: No Uniform Act baseline. Florida puts the right in the 'legally authorized person' defined in §497.005(43); §406.50 separately covers unclaimed remains. The reviewed sections have no general statutory form for naming a third party as disposition agent before death. The decedent's own written authorization comes first, then a military DD Form 93 designee, then next of kin. An attorney in fact, health surrogate, guardian or PR qualifies only as a fallback when no family member exists or is available. The end of the right is not stated in the statute.
